I basically disagree with this post.

  • I don't really know the people you are criticizing, I spend most of my time talking to people advocating for Plan C. You say the pendulum has swung too far, maybe it has, but not in the community around me as far as I can tell. I think there is still too much energy going into "oh well, let's try to make Plan C less bad, that's the best we can do" strategies relative to how much energy is going into "Let's try to make Plan A more likely" strategies. I agree it is possible to go too far, for the reasons you mention, but at least the part of the community around me doesn't seem to have gone far enough yet. YMMV.
  • I think the positive effects of a single frontier US company stopping unilaterally are larger than you or the AI forecaster think. I think that the discourse would be massively changed overnight if there was such a giant costly signal that the company actually was terrified of the risks. Also, right now even Anthropic's lobbyists seem to be pushing for weak sauce things instead of advocating for good ASI-pilled policies; if their whole company stopped development, perhaps that would also (like Cortez burning his ships) get them to pivot to advocate for better things. I agree it still probably won't work, and I don't think it's the best strategy they could take, but I hold it up as a sort of "control group" for strategies they could take, since I think every single one of these companies right now is currently pursuing a strategy that's even worse than stopping unilaterally. I don't want them to feel morally OK with what they are doing now, and I want them to know that what they are doing now is probably worse than stopping unilaterally.
  • Similarly, I think that individuals quitting the big AI companies is not necessarily the best thing they could do. Being very vocal publicly about the dangers while advocating strongly for change internally, until you get fired, seems like it could be even better. However, I think quitting and speaking up is an excellent baseline to compare strategies against, and historically it seems like most full-time-safety people inside the companies have failed to beat this baseline. (And it's even more clear for the full-time-capabilities people.) And the reason they have failed to beat this baseline is that they have convinced themselves that they are pursuing a more sophisticated and effective strategy of achieving change on the inside and putting themselves in a good position for later etc. I want to throw cold water in their faces and get them to think more clearly about whether what they are doing really is better than the baseline or not.
  • I think corporate incentives basically ARE the One Ring with massive corrupting influence. However, I also agree that mass movement politics can be like this too. However, for most individuals, it's pretty clear which corrupting influence is stronger. Ask yourself questions like the following: Am I inside an AI company's offices right now? Have I been inside such offices in the last month? Check my bank account -- where is the money coming from? List my top ten friends, and the most recent ten people I talked to. How many of them work at AI companies? OK, what about fancy think tanks that cultivate relationships with the big AI companies? OK, on the flip side: Have I been to an anti-AI protest in the last month? Have I ever? Have I ever said anything in public like "The companies should stop unilaterally? How about in the last week? Have I ever shunned anyone for working at an AI company? If I got a job at an AI company tomorrow to work on AI safety stuff, would my friends shun me?" By asking and answering simple questions like this, I think you'll pretty quickly be able to figure out which corrupting influence is more applicable to you. We each should try to resist the corrupting influence that applies most strongly to us.

Was a philosophy PhD student, left to work at AI Impacts, then Center on Long-Term Risk, then OpenAI. Quit OpenAI due to losing confidence that it would behave responsibly around the time of AGI. Now executive director of the AI Futures Project, coauthor of AI-2027 and AI-2040: Plan A. I subscribe to Crocker's Rules and am especially interested to hear unsolicited constructive criticism. http://sl4.org/crocker.html

It seems like this post argues about a dichotomy "either SURA, or race & align". E.g. your counterfactual is "Anthropic disbanded their entire company immediately with the explicit goal of raising awareness of a pause". But this dichotomy doesn't make sense to me even under your assumptions, as an answer to "What should Anthropic do?". For example, here's a different thing that Anthropic could do:

  • Stay at the frontier in order to do frontier-level alignment research, but don't release leading models. (If you're going to say, well, they need to make money--do they? Is second place not making money? If second place doesn't make much money, and really it's just Anthropic and OpenAI neck-and-neck, doesn't that somewhat put the lie to "Anthropic is barely making the race go faster."?)
  • Clearly, repeatedly, strongly commit to a conditional, indefinite stop on all frontier AI R&D.
  • Support strong binding regulation on AI R&D.
  • Aggressively publicly advocate for a global stop. Fine, make it conditional. But an actual stop, advocated clearly and consistently.
  • Actively build bridges with other AI research groups.
  • Aggressively negotiate for a stop with other research groups.
  • Other stuff that one thinks of when one sincerely wants to stop and then actually tries, as opposed to insincerely.

And on a smaller scale, I for one am, I suppose, a SURA guy, but I also encourage people to stay and seriously investigate how to get a stop / why their lab can't stop / who to organize with to get a stop / how to talk to other labs. You seem to have a lot of energy for defending that they should keep doing AI R&D, and seem to only mention

I would hope the people we're talking about (the most alignment-pilled people at major companies) would be doing anti-AI activism, and donating some of their money to anti-AI activism, regardless of whether or not they quit. All quitting does is give them less of a platform and less money.

in the comments in order to counter the argument that it would be impactful if all these people quit and advocated for a stop. You hope that they would do that, great, me too--where's the energy for that?

Your section "V.A: Getting companies to agree to stop in a coordinated manner" seems to somewhat agree with the spirit of this. But if Anthropic are the good guys, why aren't they doing this?

How much has Anthropic as a whole spent on getting a pause? It has $billions in spending and thousands of employees. What do we have from it, supporting a pause? A few essays, a paper or two, and other bits and bobs? Where's the staffed team? Where's the sustained inter-lab and international outreach? Where's the PR campaign for a stop? Where's the lobbying for an actual stop? This is not even a defensible effort, let alone a sincere and serious effort.

You say:

My very preliminary model would be that this halves our chance of getting that 20%pp bonus of going from Plan D -> Plan C+ (and so costs us 10%pp).

But what about the chances that Anthropic will safetywash / sanitywash pushing forward RSI? What about the chances that the main difference between them and OpenAI is that they'll do more handwringing and have slightly better "alignment"-patching and warning-shot masking? What about if they maneuver so that they get to continue doing AI R&D, at the cost of a pause, in the name of "well maybe the pause won't be perfect and so we'd be giving up our precious lead"?

If someone is really, truly forced to pick up into their own hands the tools to destroy the entire world, ok. But they should be terrified of this, and should seek at all times, with as much energy as they can spare, to get out of that situation!

I'm a proponent of SURA, and didn't find much to update on in this post.

According to me, the core issues are 1) whether or not the company alignment plans will succeed and 2) how close we are to the point of no return. On the first point, I think it is very low, for detailed reasons, and I think somewhat more importantly even if you take the company self-reports at face value it is substantially lower than is legitimate to accept. You, as a patient considering a cure to aging, might accept a 10% chance of death in exchange for immortality, but making that trade for everyone at once is the sort of thing that probably ought to be put to a vote. (And an independent panel of experts might think there's a substantially higher than 10% chance of failure.)

I also think we are uncomfortably close to some points of no return. Current attempts at RSI only deliver modest speedup; if there is a 'sharp left turn', we haven't hit it yet. But even if we don't have lightning-fast takeoff, many people at the labs suspect that the models will be able to replace them at some point in the next year, at which point employees lose all of them leverage on the labs. Once there are models capable of autonomously replicating on the internet, I don't expect that on its own to cause humans to lose mastery over the Earth--but it does seem like we might have to shut down the Internet, which would make us substantially poorer. (And, obviously, we could hit the sharp left turn, and end up with a second species substantially smarter than humanity, and then it forces handoff.)

MIRI developed an international agreement on the premise that we only wanted to do plans that would work, and unilateral disarmament wasn't durably effective. But if you have to halt the escalation of AI capabilities in 2027, and an international agreement can't be negotiated that fast, better for the US to halt and then focus all of its attention on getting China to halt before China reaches the cliff than to just drive off the cliff.[1]

I think that there is an 'intersection plan'--that is, both Plan A and Plan S have the same initial policy proposal (halt, set up a regulatory regime, and then unpause in a controlled way). I think it makes sense to postpone most of our arguments about whether or not AI can be used for AI alignment research until that regulatory regime exists to evaluate those arguments.


It feels like this post is trying to argue that non-experts, who may have gotten their impressions of the field from osmosis from MIRI, should instead have a more balanced information diet. I'm most sympathetic to the point about carcinization, but also it makes a lot of this post somewhat frustrating to argue with. Yeah, it sucks that you talked to a SURA proponent who didn't realize that race dynamics were relevant, but--I do realize that the race dynamics are relevant, and I still think it makes sense to push for SURA.

Similarly, it seems good for people to understand that the experts have a wide range of opinions on alignment, but I think it is underappreciated that SURA is the mainstream response to the median expert view. See Vance saying "If you're building Frankenstein, stop." or Jensen Huang saying that if we can't control our creations, we need to shut the labs because the cost to humanity is too great.

Actions speak louder than words; people see Anthropic and OpenAI putting a revolver to their temple and say "well, surely that means it's not loaded". They will notice if people drop the revolver in revulsion and horror!

This post makes plenty of good points, but I think your argument against racing to superintelligence being deontologically evil is weak. Roughly speaking, you draw an analogy between developing AI and using AI as a consumer. There's a few things I could say about that analogy directly:

-The first is that the analogy has some merit, and that I don't really feel amazing about my own heavy AI use. And I have at least one friend who has never used an LLM, explicitly because he doesn't want to contribute in any way to the race to superintelligence and human extinction. Maybe some people would call his choice foolish, but I have a lot of respect for it.

-The second thing is that there's billions of users of AI, but only thousands/maybe tens of thousands of frontier AI developers. It makes a lot more sense to try to coordinate some kind of prohibition at the latter level and than at the former. And independent of the mechanics of a boycott, I think everyone has a reasonable understanding that the developers of AI bear a lot more individual responsibility for outcomes around AI than consumers do.

But mostly, I think this deontological prohibition thing deserves more of your attention than you currently seem to be interested in giving it. There's a lot to be said about the merits of deontology vs consequentialism and how they might apply to a situation like this one, but one thing I want to focus on in particular is that deontology is "normie ethics," and when you're considering doing something that will affect everyone, including every normie, it's important to take into account how they will see it.

The analogy I'd choose is driving. It's hard to define exactly what it means to be a good or bad driver, but at least as important as raw skill is predictability, by which I mean how predictable you are to everyone else. If you drive 30 above the speed limit on the highway, weaving between lanes to pass the other cars, is that fine so long as you are skilled enough to avoid an accident? Is it fine to run a red light at night when there's no one else around? Maybe it is, I guess. But I'd point out that that kind of strategy is brittle. It makes you unpredictable to everyone else. If something unexpected (to you) happens, your strategy fails catastrophically.

In the same way, I think normies are baffled, confused, and repulsed by the thing where Anthropic employees, despite having p(doom)s, continue working on the tech anyway. The most common sentiment I hear, once I've fully explained the situation and insisted that no, it's not them hyping, it's not about the IPO, this is something they really truly believe, is "those people should be arrested."

I want to be very clear: I don't agree that Anthropic employees should be arrested. I'm not even sure they're doing the wrong thing. This is a complicated and cursed situation, it's genuinely unclear what the right approach is, I believe them that they are doing the right thing according to their own model of the world, and I feel a lot of empathy for them. But they're the equivalent of a weirdo driver on the road. Nobody else is expecting this behavior from them. This is why the canard of "they're doing it for the hype" just won't die, even though it fails to even the most basic scrutiny: it's because the truth, that they really do think that AI might kill us all, and that the best way to stop it might be to build the AI even faster, sounds so insane to a normal person not steeped in our weird culture as to be self-evidently absurd.

In your open letter to Steven Pinker, you wrote:

When Anthropic decided that the best way to forestall the AI apocalypse was to make a desperate push beyond the existing scientific frontier and create the dangerous AI themselves so they could be sure to get the technology right, with limitless benefits for humanity if they succeeded, you … played it for laughs, asking tongue-in-cheek “Why are the same people who warn that a technology will kill us all building it as fast as they can?”

I saw that this particular passage of your post was making the rounds on X among people hostile to you and the cause of EA/AI safety in general. Generally people would quote it and say something like, "Look how crazy they are. Look at the the degree to which Scott has drunk the Kool-Aid. This is self-evidently insane."

Again: I don't agree. I understand where Anthropic is coming from. I don't think these Twitter dunks were in good faith.

But: there's a reason that passage in particular was chosen by your opponents as the part of the post that would make you look craziest. And it made you look crazy because, to most people, Anthropic's entire strategy, its entire raison d'etre, looks crazy. It makes them take Anthropic's warnings a lot less seriously. And, like, that is a real problem. You make a lot of good points about why it makes sense for Anthropic to exist anyway. I don't have a lot of great answers to those points. But there's a serious problem here, it's downstream of this "if you have high ASI p(doom), racing to superintelligence is obviously deontologically prohibited" thing, that most people would not necessarily put in those terms but which they do strongly feel. So I think it maybe deserves a more serious response from you (sorry, I know your post was already very long and that I'm proposing it should be even longer). Like, it is just true that consequentialism can be used to justify basically anything power-seeking so long as you protest that you will use your power wisely. And it is also true that deontology, while flawed, is the only tool we have for how to make ethical decisions using corrupted hardware.
